answer: The plan is strong on problem clarity and early traction, but the written submission has several fixable weaknesses. (1) Tighten and substantiate the market sizing: the '$100M+' figure rests on an arbitrary 25% adoption assumption for a one-time purchase. Replace with a bottom-up, time-bound model (e.g., realistic share of 12M households reachable via channels, conversion rates from the 400-person waitlist and pilot data) and show SAM/SOM, not just TAM. (2) Strengthen the evidence: the 14% temperature-loss reduction and 8-12% bill savings are small-sample (41 apartments), self-reported, and confounded by weather; add control comparisons, weather-normalization, absolute dollar savings per household, and payback time on the $59 kit. State the survey method and sample limits (212 students is not representative of renters). Report pilot conversion and retention: 27 paid of 41 is good, but how many completed three fixes, reran scans, or would repurchase? (3) Resolve the business-model tension: sensors are reusable and can be lent between units, which undercuts one-time kit sales; explain why renters keep buying and why the $6/unit/month subscription is justified versus a one-time scan. Provide unit economics: CAC, gross margin after returns/support/shipping/payments, LTV, and subscription churn. At $59 vs. $24 COGS, margin looks fine on paper but fully loaded margin is not shown. (4) Clarify landlord incentives: the plan acknowledges landlords lack bills and motivation, yet relies on them as the recurring revenue engine from one 12-unit paid pilot. Explain who benefits (tenant pays bills), why landlords pay, and what evidence beyond one pilot supports willingness to pay. Consider that landlords may resist tenant-generated data on building defects. (5) Quantify the data-licensing and utility claims or de-emphasize them: utility sales cycles are long, privacy, consent, and data-quality issues are unaddressed, and the year-two utility pilot looks speculative. Name any utility conversations held. (6) Make financials credible: the revenue projection ($85K to $420K) lacks assumptions (units sold, prices, subscriber counts, growth drivers). Provide a simple model, a cost/expense forecast, runway, and break-even, not just revenue. Note the 800-kit run is roughly $19K at current COGS yet projected year-one revenue implies far more units than that; reconcile production quantity with sales goals. (7) Address risks and gaps explicitly: hardware certification (FCC/UL), battery safety, reliability and accuracy of low-cost sensors versus validated references, customer support burden, returns, and inventory risk. Discuss defensibility beyond 'data over time': the sensor-plus-software combination is replicable, so specify IP, algorithm validation, proprietary dataset scale, and switching costs. Also address competitors like Sense, Samsung/Ecobee, and cheaper DIY thermometer/IR gun approaches. (8) Show team and execution readiness: all members are students and none has hardware manufacturing or sales experience; state full-time commitment, equity split, and the plan to fill gaps (manufacturing mentor, sales lead). Incorporate before launch and clarify IP ownership given the university grant and faculty involvement. (9) Sharpen the ask: justify $40K line by line (800 kits, certification cost, legal, insurance, marketing), define milestones the money buys (kits sold, landlord units under contract, validated savings), and explain the path to follow-on funding or sustainability. (10) Presentation: lead with the strongest proof (paid pilots, measured savings), add a customer acquisition plan (specific channels, partnerships with property associations, cost per acquisition), include a one-page visual of the user journey and a sample heat-loss output, cite sources for market numbers (44M renters, 2M small landlords), and trim repetition so the summary stays concise and every claim is backed by a number or source.
